clue.text: Musical's enraging tune you altered

indicators.note: something altered has been changed, so the preceding words are rearranged

parts.note: the three words taken letter for letter

explanation.surface: A show whose irritating melody you have tinkered with.
explanation.walkthrough: ANNIE GET YOUR GUN is the Irving Berlin show about the sharpshooter Annie Oakley.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a famous Broadway stage show with songs, so an example of a musical.

clue.text: Country's opera song enthralling people

indicators.note: to enthral is to hold captive, so one piece holds the other inside it

parts.note: an aria is a solo song in an opera
men are people

explanation.surface: A nation's operatic number captivates its audience.
explanation.definitionFit: Armenia is a nation in the Caucasus, an instance of a country.

clue.text: Nine musicians? No, flipping ten

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: flipping something over turns it end to end, so the word after it reads backwards

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone insists a band has nine players, not ten, with mild exasperation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flipping' looks like a mild British expletive, but it turns the ten round.
explanation.definitionFit: A nonet is a group of nine performers; the question mark flags that it can also mean a piece for them.

clue.text: Public schoolboys welcoming southern Europeans

indicators.note: welcoming someone means taking them in, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: pupils of Eton, the famous English public (fee-paying) school
S is the abbreviation for southern

explanation.surface: Pupils at a posh school greet visitors from the south of the continent.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain a public school is an exclusive private one, and Eton is the best known.
explanation.definitionFit: Estonians are the people of a Baltic nation, so they are Europeans.

clue.text: Racecourse records only matter initially

parts.note: EPs are extended-play records

indicators.note: initially points to the opening letter of each of the words before it

parts.note: the opening letters of these two words

explanation.surface: At the track, only the form book counts.
explanation.walkthrough: EPSOM is the Surrey racecourse where the Derby is run.
explanation.definitionFit: Epsom Downs is a famous horse-racing venue, an example of a racecourse.

clue.text: Longs to skip English tales

indicators.note: to skip something is to leave it out, so a letter is dropped from the word

parts.note: longs as a verb, to yearn
E is the abbreviation for English

explanation.surface: A wish to avoid hearing English stories.
explanation.definitionFit: Yarns are long rambling stories, so a synonym for tales.

clue.text: Employment in America for one returning

parts.note: the usual abbreviation for the United States of America

indicators.note: returning means going back the way one came, so the letters for the phrase before it read backwards

parts.note: e.g. means for example, i.e. for one

explanation.surface: Jobs in the US for someone coming back home.
explanation.walkthrough: 'For one' is the standard way to clue e.g.
explanation.definitionFit: Usage means the act of using something, which is a sense of employment as in the employment of a tool.

clue.text: Sanguine, a pigeon traps rodent

indicators.note: the words before it trap or hold the answer inside them

parts.note: found across these words, ignoring the comma

explanation.surface: An optimistic pigeon catches a small animal.
explanation.definitionFit: A guinea pig is a cavy, a small domesticated rodent kept as a pet.

clue.text: Fan runs into Tiger Woods's supporter Hazel?

parts.note: a nut is an enthusiast, as in a golf nut

indicators.note: going into something puts one letter inside the other piece

parts.note: a golfer like Tiger Woods rests the ball on a tee
R is the cricket abbreviation for runs

explanation.surface: A golf fan gets in among the golfer's backers, who include someone called Hazel.
explanation.walkthrough: Tiger Woods suggests golf fans, but his supporter is the little peg the ball sits on.
explanation.definitionFit: A hazel is a tree that bears hazelnuts, an example of a nut tree; the question mark flags the example.

clue.text: Finally you went, entering pits for short periods

indicators.note: entering means going inside, so those letters sit within the next piece

parts.note: mines are pits dug for coal

indicators.note: finally points to the closing letter of each of the two words that follow

parts.note: the closing letters of these two words

explanation.surface: In the end you went down the coal pits for brief spells.
explanation.definitionFit: Minutes are sixty-second units of time, brief spans.

clue.text: One who's pragmatic about a catalogue

parts.note: re means concerning
taken as written
a list is a catalogue

explanation.surface: A practical person comments on a product catalogue.
explanation.definitionFit: A realist is a person who deals with things as they are, a practical sort.

clue.text: Either way it's unacceptable

indicators.note: either way means read forwards or backwards, so the letters are the same in both directions

parts.note: a two-word informal phrase for this, which reads identically from both ends

explanation.surface: Whichever way you look at it, this is not allowed.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition itself supplies the letters; the indicator adds that they read the same in both directions.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Not on' is British slang for not acceptable, as in 'that's just not on'.

clue.text: Soldier must reek badly, having been injected with drug

indicators.note: an injection puts something inside, so one letter goes into the rearranged letters
badly suggests the words are mangled into a different order

parts.note: the two words taken letter for letter
E is slang for the drug ecstasy

explanation.surface: A soldier who has been on drugs must smell terrible.
explanation.definitionFit: A musketeer was an infantryman armed with a musket, so a soldier.

clue.text: Grubby family member aunt regularly ignored

parts.note: an uncle is a relative

indicators.note: ignoring every other letter at regular intervals keeps only the alternate ones

parts.note: first and third letters of the word

explanation.surface: A scruffy relative is always overlooked by his aunt.
explanation.definitionFit: Unclean means dirty, a synonym of grubby.

clue.text: Delight and disgust when touring Ecuador's capital

indicators.note: touring means going all round, so one word surrounds a letter

parts.note: to appal is to disgust

indicators.note: a capital is the head, here meaning the first letter of the name

parts.note: the opening letter of the country's name

explanation.surface: A traveller in Quito feels both pleasure and revulsion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ecuador's capital' looks like Quito, but it is just the country's first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: To appeal is to attract or please, so a verb meaning delight.

clue.text: Wide-ranging fear about old sheep

indicators.note: about means around, so one word goes round the next pieces

parts.note: panic is sudden fear
O is the abbreviation for old
a ram is a male sheep

explanation.surface: Widespread alarm concerning an elderly sheep.
explanation.definitionFit: Panoramic describes a sweeping, all-embracing view, so far-reaching or broad.

clue.text: Upset close pal and break down

indicators.note: something upset is knocked over and disordered, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: the two words taken letter for letter

explanation.surface: Someone distressed their best friend, who then broke down in tears.
explanation.definitionFit: To collapse is to fail or give way, the same as to break down.

clue.text: Call round after work to find missing peer

indicators.note: letters put to work are processed and reshaped, so they come out in a new order

parts.note: the two words taken letter for letter

explanation.surface: Phone round once the working day is done to track down a vanished aristocrat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Round' looks like part of the instruction, but it is fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Lord Lucan, a British earl, vanished in 1974 after his children's nanny was murdered and was never found.

clue.text: Good-looking husband one's mad to change

parts.note: H is the abbreviation for husband

indicators.note: to change the words is to alter their order

parts.note: the words taken letter for letter

explanation.surface: An attractive husband: anyone would be crazy to swap him.
explanation.definitionFit: Handsome means attractive in appearance, a synonym.

clue.text: Promising help, UFO goes off

indicators.note: something that goes off explodes or spoils, so the letters fly apart into a new order

parts.note: the two words taken letter for letter

explanation.surface: An offer of assistance just as a flying saucer departs.
explanation.definitionFit: Hopeful describes something showing promise of success, as in a hopeful sign.

clue.text: British bad guy's accent

parts.note: B is the abbreviation for British
a rogue is a villain

explanation.surface: The villain in a film speaks with an English voice.
explanation.definitionFit: A brogue is a strong regional accent, especially an Irish one.

clue.text: Ruler and politician admitted to base, heartless error

indicators.note: being admitted means being let inside, so one piece is placed within the others
without a heart means the central letter of the word is removed

parts.note: taken as written
Member of Parliament
e is the base of natural logarithms

explanation.surface: A monarch and a lawmaker let into a lowly place, through a careless mistake.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Base' is the mathematical constant e; error loses its middle R, and the politician slips in after that E.
explanation.definitionFit: An emperor is the sovereign of an empire, a supreme ruler.

clue.text: Continuing exercise, chap comes in ripped

parts.note: PE is physical education

indicators.note: coming in means entering, so one piece goes inside the next

parts.note: rent is an old past participle of rend, to tear
a chap is a man

explanation.surface: A man arrives for a workout looking muscular.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ripped' tempts as gym slang for muscular, but here it means torn.
explanation.definitionFit: Permanent means lasting or ongoing indefinitely, so continuing.

clue.text: Exhausted, Tallinn's out of bounds

indicators.note: the bounds are the edges, so the word's outer letters are put out

parts.note: the Estonian capital, taken as written

explanation.surface: A tired visitor finds the Estonian capital is a no-go area.
explanation.definitionFit: All in is an informal phrase for completely worn out, so exhausted.

clue.text: Gently moves tea sets with no time at all

indicators.note: with no means lacking, so the following letter is taken away wherever it appears

parts.note: taken as written
T is the abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: Someone carefully shifts the crockery in a hurry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'At all' says every T goes, all three of them.
explanation.definitionFit: To ease something is to manoeuvre it carefully into place, so gently moves.

clue.text: Tense hour with strange drone

parts.note: T is the grammar abbreviation for tense
H is the abbreviation for hour
rum is British slang for odd

explanation.surface: An anxious sixty minutes with an odd humming noise.
explanation.definitionFit: A thrum is a continuous low humming sound, the same as a drone.

clue.text: Eagerly accept the French doggy

parts.note: la is French for the (feminine)
a pup is a young dog

explanation.surface: A French dog keen to take whatever it is given.
explanation.definitionFit: To lap up is to accept eagerly, an idiom from a dog lapping its food.

clue.text: Central point brought up to guest of honour

indicators.note: in a down entry, bringing letters up makes them read from bottom to top

parts.note: taken as written
a very important person

explanation.surface: The main issue is raised with the guest of honour.
explanation.definitionFit: A pivot is the fixed point on which something turns, so a central point.

clue.text: Mishandles rages, suppressing extremists from Bristol

indicators.note: suppressing means holding down inside, so one piece is enclosed by the other

parts.note: to fume is to rage

indicators.note: extremists are at the far ends, so only the first and last letters of the name are kept

parts.note: the outer letters of the city's name

explanation.surface: A politician bungles matters, seething while silencing radicals in Bristol.
explanation.definitionFit: To fumble is to handle clumsily, a synonym of mishandle.

clue.text: Get better free, unlimited insurance

indicators.note: without limits means the edge letters go, leaving only the inner ones

parts.note: the inner two letters of the word
insurance cover

explanation.surface: Recuperate with free, unlimited health insurance.
explanation.definitionFit: To recover is to return to health, the same as getting better.

clue.text: Ron lost chessmen, playing legend from Scotland

indicators.note: pieces in play are moved about, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: the three words taken letter for letter

explanation.surface: Ron loses pieces during a game, perhaps to a famous Scot.
explanation.definitionFit: The Loch Ness Monster is a mythical creature said to live in a Scottish lake, a Highland folk tale.
